newsitem.title: UK: Debt supply to weigh on Germany, France.
newsitem.headline: Debt supply to weigh on Germany, France.

text.p: A chunky diet of debt will weigh heaviest on Germany and France in 1997, pushing up yields in a vulnerable market early this year, analysts said on Friday.

"You've seen some back-up in yields in the past couple of weeks (in France and Germany) but these levels are not overly attractive to domestic investors," said Sonia Gibbs, senior bond strategist at Nomura International. "It may be a tougher sell."
Bright spots on the supply front include Sweden and Denmark, where redemptions are set to fall in 1997. In the trend-setting U.S. market, there is no major auction until late January.

A new 10-year Bund will be the highlight of early January but with yields at low levels, analysts do not expect the debt to be eagerly taken up. Bunds have a sizeable yield discount to Treasuries, having outpaced the U.S. market throughout 1996.
The 10-year U.S./German yield gap was at 65 basis points (0.65 percentage point) at 1230 GMT.
"The German market has outperformed the U.S. by a big margin. I think supply will be a problem," said Kirit Shah, chief strategist at Sanwa International in London.
Shah said investors would look to the new Bunds as a benchmark to readjust their portfolios. But he also said German yields would need to rise to attract demand.
Others agreed and said the current wave of supply was not coming at a particularly good time. Recent auctions of French and Italian debt had not been overwhelmingly popular, they said.

The German government in late December released plans for first-quarter debt issuance of as much as 54 billion marks ($34.9 billion), including a 10-year Bund totaling as much as 15 billion in the first 10 days of January.
"The market is vulnerable to bad news and the supply is one of the factors that is dangerous," said Gerlof de Vrej, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.

De Vrej said the current steepness of the German yield curve could offer some protection for the market. German three-month deposits currently yield 3.05 percent, against 5.96 percent for 10-year debt.

But he said Bunds still remained susceptible to price declines. A knee-jerk fall on Friday on the back of industrial production data, which in previous months has not been a market-mover, demonstrated this, he said. "The market is not too strong at the moment. The sentiment is quite bad."
One reason why so much supply is on the way is that a lot of old bonds are coming due this year. France, as well as Germany, will suffer for that reason, analysts said.

The French finance ministry earlier this week said it planned to sell about 600 billion francs ($115 billion) of medium and long-term debt in 1997, up from a little over 560 billion in 1996. Redemptions are set to climb about 100 billion francs to more than 350 billion francs in the coming year.
By the same token, Sweden and Denmark look set to have few issuance problems as supply in those countries is on the wane, Gibbs said. "For me the bright spots are Denmark and Sweden."

Danish gross issuance could decline from more than 100 billion crowns ($16.9 billion) in 1996 to roughly 70 billion this year, Gibbs said. She estimated redemptions would decline to 65 billion this year from 85 billion last, while the deficit was set to fall to around six billion crowns from a little over 19 billion.

In the short term, investors can also look forward to long-dated debt auctions next week in Spain and a French monthly Ecu debt auction. But the real litmus test on the supply front, the next U.S. 10-year auction, is not until January 29.
($1=5.230 French Franc)
($1=5.911 Danish Crown)
